# Running Your Expo App on Android from Windows (Phone or Emulator)

This guide walks you through every step of creating an Expo app on your Windows PC and running it on either a **physical Android phone** or an **Android emulator** (a simulated phone that runs on your computer). Unlike iOS development, Android development is completely free — no paid developer accounts required.

> **What you'll need:** A Windows PC, and either an Android phone with a USB cable or enough disk space (~10 GB) for Android Studio and an emulator.

---

## Part 1: Install the Required Tools

You need three things on your Windows machine: **Node.js**, a **Java Development Kit (JDK)**, and **Android Studio**. We'll install them in order.

### 1.1 — Install Node.js

Node.js is the engine that runs JavaScript outside a web browser — it powers all of the Expo tooling.

1. Go to [https://nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org) in your browser.
2. Download the **LTS** (Long Term Support) version. As of this writing, that's version 22.x.
3. Run the installer. Accept the defaults and click through until it finishes.

To verify it worked, open **PowerShell** (search for "PowerShell" in the Start menu) and type:

```powershell
node --version
```

You should see something like `v22.x.x`. Anything 22.11.0 or higher is fine.

> **What is PowerShell?** It's Windows' built-in command line tool — similar to Terminal on a Mac. You'll use it throughout this guide to run commands. You can also use the older "Command Prompt" app; either works.

### 1.2 — Install the Java Development Kit (JDK)

React Native (the framework Expo is built on) needs Java to compile Android apps. We'll use Chocolatey (a package manager for Windows) to install it cleanly.

#### First, install Chocolatey:

1. Open PowerShell **as Administrator**: right-click the PowerShell icon in the Start menu and select **Run as administrator**.
2. Paste this command and press Enter:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process -Force; [System.Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [System.Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor 3072; iex ((New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://community.chocolatey.org/install.ps1'))
```

3. Wait for it to finish, then close and reopen PowerShell (as Administrator again).

#### Then install the JDK:

```powershell
choco install -y microsoft-openjdk17
```

This installs OpenJDK 17, which is the recommended version. Close and reopen PowerShell when it finishes.

### 1.3 — Install Android Studio

Android Studio is the official development environment for Android. Even though you'll write your code in VS Code, Android Studio provides the compiler, emulator, and SDK tools needed to build Android apps.

1. Go to [https://developer.android.com/studio](https://developer.android.com/studio) and download Android Studio.
2. Run the installer. When you reach the **Choose Components** screen, make sure all boxes are checked, especially:
   - Android SDK
   - Android SDK Platform
   - Android Virtual Device
3. Click **Next** and let it install everything.
4. When Android Studio finishes installing and opens for the first time, it will download additional components. Let it finish — this can take several minutes.

#### Install the correct Android SDK version

1. On the Android Studio welcome screen, click **More Actions** (or the three-dot menu) and select **SDK Manager**.
2. In the **SDK Platforms** tab, check the box next to **Show Package Details** in the bottom-right corner.
3. Find and expand **Android 15 (VanillaIceCream)**. Make sure these are checked:
   - `Android SDK Platform 35`
   - `Google APIs Intel x86 Atom_64 System Image` (or `Google APIs ARM 64 v8a System Image` if you have an ARM-based Windows machine)
4. Switch to the **SDK Tools** tab. Check **Show Package Details** again. Expand **Android SDK Build-Tools** and make sure `36.0.0` is checked. Also make sure **Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)** is checked.
5. Click **Apply**, then **OK** to download and install everything.

#### Set the ANDROID_HOME environment variable

The build tools need to know where the Android SDK is installed. Here's how to tell them:

1. Open the **Start menu** and search for **"Environment Variables"**. Click **Edit the system environment variables**.
2. In the window that appears, click the **Environment Variables** button near the bottom.
3. Under **User variables** (the top section), click **New** and enter:
   - **Variable name:** `ANDROID_HOME`
   - **Variable value:** `C:\Users\YOUR_USERNAME\AppData\Local\Android\Sdk`
   
   (Replace `YOUR_USERNAME` with your actual Windows username. If you're unsure of the path, open Android Studio → Settings → Languages & Frameworks → Android SDK — the path is shown at the top.)
4. Still in User variables, find the variable called **Path**, select it, and click **Edit**.
5. Click **New** and add: `%ANDROID_HOME%\platform-tools`
6. Click **New** again and add: `%ANDROID_HOME%\emulator`
7. Click **OK** on all dialogs to save.
8. **Close and reopen PowerShell** so the new variables take effect.

Verify it worked:

```powershell
echo $env:ANDROID_HOME
```

It should print the path to your SDK folder.

---

## Part 2: Create Your Expo Project

### 2.1 — Create the project

Open PowerShell (a normal window, not Administrator) and navigate to wherever you want your project to live. Your Desktop is fine:

```powershell
cd ~\Desktop
npx create-expo-app MyFirstApp
cd MyFirstApp
```

The first command downloads a template and sets up a complete starter project in a folder called `MyFirstApp`. The `cd` command moves you into that folder. (If prompted to install `create-expo-app`, type `y` and press Enter.)

### 2.2 — Install the development client library

This turns your app into a "development build" — your own custom version of the Expo Go playground with full native capabilities:

```powershell
npx expo install expo-dev-client
```

### 2.3 — Open the project in VS Code

```powershell
code .
```

(The `.` means "the current folder.") You can browse and edit your app's source files here. The main file you'll edit is `app/(tabs)/index.tsx` or `App.js`, depending on the template.

---

## Part 3: Option A — Run on a Physical Android Phone

Using a real phone is the best way to see exactly what your users will experience. You'll connect your phone via USB and the build tool will install the app directly.

### 3A.1 — Enable Developer Options on your phone

Android hides its developer settings by default. To unlock them:

1. On your phone, go to **Settings → About phone** (on some phones it's under Settings → System → About phone).
2. Find **Build number** and **tap it 7 times** in a row.
3. You'll see a message saying "You are now a developer!" (You may need to enter your phone's PIN.)

### 3A.2 — Enable USB Debugging

1. Go back to **Settings**. You should now see **Developer options** (sometimes under Settings → System).
2. Open **Developer options** and toggle on **USB debugging**.
3. A confirmation dialog will appear — tap **OK**.

### 3A.3 — Connect your phone to your PC

1. Plug your phone into your PC with a USB cable.
2. A prompt will appear on your phone: **"Allow USB debugging?"** — tap **Allow**. Check "Always allow from this computer" if you want to skip this next time.

To verify the connection, run in PowerShell:

```powershell
adb devices
```

You should see your device listed with the word `device` next to it. (The `adb` tool was installed as part of the Android SDK platform-tools.) If you see `unauthorized`, check your phone for the USB debugging prompt and tap Allow.

### 3A.4 — Build and run

In PowerShell, make sure you're inside your project folder (`~\Desktop\MyFirstApp`) and run:

```powershell
npx expo run:android --device
```

Here's what happens behind the scenes:

1. **Prebuild**: It generates a native Android project (an `android` folder) from your Expo configuration.
2. **Compile**: It uses the Android SDK (installed with Android Studio) to compile that native project into an APK.
3. **Install**: It installs the APK onto your connected phone and launches it.

If you have multiple devices available (phone + emulator), it will ask you to pick one — use the arrow keys and press Enter.

**The first build takes a while** — typically **5 to 15 minutes** — because it compiles all the native code from scratch. You'll see lots of output scrolling in PowerShell. As long as you don't see a red **BUILD FAILED**, it's working. Be patient.

---

## Part 3: Option B — Run on an Android Emulator

If you don't have an Android phone (or just want to test on your computer screen), you can create a virtual phone that runs on your PC.

### 3B.1 — Create an Android Virtual Device (AVD)

1. Open **Android Studio**.
2. On the welcome screen, click **More Actions** → **Virtual Device Manager** (may also be called "AVD Manager" or "Device Manager").
3. Click **Create Virtual Device**.
4. Pick a phone model from the list (e.g., **Pixel 8**) and click **Next**.
5. Select the **VanillaIceCream** (API Level 35) system image. If it has a download icon, click it to download first, then select it and click **Next**.
6. Click **Finish**.

### 3B.2 — Launch the emulator

In the Virtual Device Manager, click the **green play button** (▶) next to your new device. A virtual phone will appear on screen. The first launch takes a minute or two.

### 3B.3 — Build and run

With the emulator running, go to PowerShell, make sure you're in your project folder, and run:

```powershell
npx expo run:android
```

(Without `--device`, it will automatically find the running emulator.)

It will compile the app and install it on the emulator. The first build takes **5 to 15 minutes**. After it finishes, the app will launch automatically in the emulator window.

---

## Part 4: Develop Your App

### 4.1 — The development workflow

After the initial build, you generally **do not need to rebuild** every time you change code. Here's the typical cycle:

1. Edit your JavaScript/TypeScript files in VS Code.
2. Save the file.
3. The app on your phone or emulator **updates automatically** within seconds (this is called "Fast Refresh").

If the development server isn't running (for example, you closed PowerShell), restart it without rebuilding:

```powershell
npx expo start
```

Then press `a` in the terminal to launch the app on your connected Android device or emulator.

### 4.2 — When you DO need to rebuild

You only need to run `npx expo run:android` again if you:

- Add or remove a native library (e.g., camera, maps, push notifications).
- Change something in `app.json` / `app.config.js` that affects native configuration (app name, icon, permissions, etc.).

For day-to-day JavaScript/TypeScript work, just save and watch it refresh.

### 4.3 — Network requirements

The development server sends your JavaScript code to the device over your local network.

- **Emulator**: This happens automatically — no special setup needed.
- **Physical phone**: Your phone and PC must be on the **same Wi-Fi network**. If that's not possible (for example, on a campus network that blocks device-to-device traffic), you can use USB forwarding instead by running this command in a separate PowerShell window:

```powershell
adb reverse tcp:8081 tcp:8081
```

This routes traffic through the USB cable instead of Wi-Fi.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

**"adb is not recognized as a command"**: The ANDROID_HOME environment variable isn't set correctly, or you need to close and reopen PowerShell after setting it. Double-check Part 1.3 (the environment variable section).

**"SDK location not found"**: Create a file called `local.properties` inside the `android` folder of your project, and add this line (with your actual path):
```
sdk.dir=C:\\Users\\YOUR_USERNAME\\AppData\\Local\\Android\\Sdk
```

**BUILD FAILED with "license not accepted"**: Run this in PowerShell and accept all licenses:
```powershell
sdkmanager --licenses
```
(If `sdkmanager` isn't found, use the full path: `"$env:ANDROID_HOME\cmdline-tools\latest\bin\sdkmanager" --licenses`)

**Emulator is extremely slow**: Make sure hardware acceleration is enabled. In Android Studio, go to SDK Manager → SDK Tools tab and check that **Intel x86 Emulator Accelerator (HAXM)** is installed (for Intel CPUs) or that **Windows Hypervisor Platform** is enabled in Windows Features (for AMD CPUs or Hyper-V). You may need to enable virtualization in your BIOS.

**Phone not appearing in `adb devices`**: Try a different USB cable (some cables are charge-only and don't support data). Make sure USB debugging is enabled. Try revoking USB debugging authorizations in Developer Options and reconnecting.

**Metro bundler can't connect to physical device**: Make sure your PC and phone are on the same Wi-Fi network, or use `adb reverse tcp:8081 tcp:8081` to route over USB.

**"Execution failed for task ':app:installDebug'"**: This sometimes means the app is already installed with a different signature. Uninstall the app from your phone/emulator and rebuild.

---

## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Create a new project | `npx create-expo-app MyApp` |
| Install dev client | `npx expo install expo-dev-client` |
| Build & run on phone | `npx expo run:android --device` |
| Build & run on emulator | `npx expo run:android` |
| Start dev server (no rebuild) | `npx expo start` |
| Route traffic over USB | `adb reverse tcp:8081 tcp:8081` |
| Clean rebuild from scratch | `npx expo prebuild --clean` then `npx expo run:android` |
| Check connected devices | `adb devices` |
